learning_objective: 🎯 Expand your mathematical universe! Discover the difference between numbers that can be written as simple fractions and the wild, never-ending 'Irrational' numbers.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A rational number can be written as a fraction $p/q$ (where $q$ is not 0). Their decimals either stop completely (like $1/2 = 0.5$) or repeat in a predictable pattern (like $1/3 = 0.333...$).
These numbers CANNOT be written as simple fractions. Their decimals go on forever without ever repeating a pattern. Famous examples are $\pi$ (Pi) and $\sqrt{2}$.
If you put all the Rational numbers and all the Irrational numbers together into one big family, you get the 'Real Numbers'. Every single point on the number line represents a unique Real Number.

fun_activity.title: 🐌 The Square Root Spiral
fun_activity.instructions: Draw a right-angled triangle with a base of 1 cm and height of 1 cm. By Pythagoras, the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$. Use that hypotenuse as the base for a new triangle (height 1 cm) to get $\sqrt{3}$. Keep going to create the beautiful Spiral of Theodorus!

exam_tips: 📌 To find a rational number between two numbers $a$ and $b$, simply average them: $(a+b)/2$.
📌 Be ready to convert repeating decimals like $0.777...$ into $p/q$ form. Let $x = 0.777...$, multiply by 10, and subtract!
📌 Remember: The sum of a rational and an irrational number is ALWAYS irrational (e.g., $2 + \sqrt{3}$).
quick_recap: ⭐ Rational numbers have terminating or non-terminating repeating decimal expansions.
⭐ Irrational numbers have non-terminating, non-repeating decimal expansions.
⭐ Real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers, filling every gap on the number line.
